# Load all libraries at once

if(!dir.exists("data/mp01")) dir.create("data/mp01", recursive=TRUE)

GLOBAL_TOP_10_FILE <- "data/mp01/global_top10_alltime.csv"
COUNTRY_TOP_10_FILE <- "data/mp01/country_top10_alltime.csv"

if(!file.exists(GLOBAL_TOP_10_FILE)){
  download.file("https://www.netflix.com/tudum/top10/data/all-weeks-global.tsv",
                destfile = GLOBAL_TOP_10_FILE)
}

if(!file.exists(COUNTRY_TOP_10_FILE)){
  download.file("https://www.netflix.com/tudum/top10/data/all-weeks-countries.tsv",
                destfile = COUNTRY_TOP_10_FILE)
}

GLOBAL_TOP_10 <- read_tsv(GLOBAL_TOP_10_FILE) %>%
  mutate(season_title = if_else(season_title == "N/A", NA_character_, season_title))

COUNTRY_TOP_10 <- read_tsv(COUNTRY_TOP_10_FILE, na = "N/A") %>%
  mutate(season_title = if_else(season_title == "N/A", NA_character_, season_title))



Introduction
Netflix is part of daily life for millions of people around the world, with everything from hit TV shows to blockbuster movies. Some titles become popular everywhere, while others are loved more in certain countries. In this project, I look at Netflix’s global and country-specific Top 10 data to find patterns in what people watch, see which shows and movies perform best, and understand how popularity changes across regions.
I study both English and non-English content, showing global hits like Stranger Things as well as local favorites that are gaining attention internationally, especially from countries like Korea and India. The goal is to give the Netflix Public Relations team clear, data-driven insights so they can tell interesting stories about their most successful content.

Press Release 1: Back to Hawkins: The Final Stranger Things Season is Coming!



Stranger Things 5


Hey Stranger Things fans! Season 5 is coming soon, and everyone is excited to go back to Hawkins, Indiana. The show has been super popular since 2016. So far, it’s been in the global Top 10 for 42 weeks and people around the world have watched over 2,043,650,000 hours of it. That’s way more than most other English-language TV shows on Netflix!
Each season keeps getting bigger. Season 4 alone got over 1.2 billion hours viewed, showing how much people love it. And it’s not just popular in the U.S.—Stranger Things hit the Top 10 in tons of countries, like in Serbia it stayed in the Top 10 for 58 weeks!
The Duffer Brothers made the show, and it’s all about a group of teens who find crazy supernatural stuff in their town. There’s also comics, books, games, and even live experiences for fans. Stranger Things is more than a show—it’s a worldwide phenomenon, and Season 5 looks like it’s going to be epic.

Press Release 2: Lights, Camera, India: Netflix’s Nonstop Growth



India Netflix


Netflix has seen incredible growth in India, with Hindi-language films and TV shows reaching millions of viewers every week. Popular programs like RRR (Hindi) and Squid Game (dubbed) have drawn huge audiences, with RRR spending 18 weeks in the global Top 10 and Squid Game: Season 1 accumulating over 2.7 billion hours viewed worldwide. In addition, Through My Window reached 18 weeks in the global Top 10, showing strong local and international engagement.
The data suggests that Netflix’s Hindi-language content is not only a hit in India but also resonates globally, highlighting a growing base of subscribers in one of the world’s largest markets. With over 200 weeks of continuous service in India, Netflix is poised to expand its influence and continue to attract viewers eager for local stories with global appeal.

    Japan_Weeks = ifelse(is.na(Japan_Weeks), 0, Japan_Weeks)
  ) |>
  select(Rank, show_title, category, India_Weeks, US_Weeks, UK_Weeks, Japan_Weeks) |>
  rename(
    Title = show_title,
    Category = category,
    `India Weeks` = India_Weeks,
    `US Weeks` = US_Weeks,

Press Release 3: Netflix Brings the World to Your Screen



Compressed Image


Netflix is proud to highlight the success of non-English-language films, showing that audiences love stories from all over the world. Films like All Quiet on the Western Front have spent 23 weeks in the global Top 10, while Pushpa 2: The Rule (Reloaded Version) became the longest film ever to make the list at 224 minutes. Other hits include Blood Red Sky (16 weeks) and K.O. (11 weeks).
These titles show that viewers are willing to watch long and diverse stories, creating opportunities for Netflix to invest in global content. Non-English films are no longer niche; they are now key drivers of international growth, capturing viewers in multiple regions and proving that a great story speaks every language.

# Join INCOME and RENT 
income_rent <- INCOME %>%

combined_data <- income_rent %>%

combined_data <- combined_data %>%
  mutate(
    rent_to_income = monthly_rent / (household_income / 12)

# Standardization
baseline <- combined_data %>%
  filter(year == min(year)) %>%
  summarize(avg = mean(rent_to_income, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pull(avg)

combined_data <- combined_data %>%
  mutate(
    rent_burden_metric = case_when(
      rent_to_income >= baseline ~ 
        50 + 50 * (rent_to_income - baseline) / (max(rent_to_income, na.rm = TRUE) - baseline),
      rent_to_income < baseline ~ 
        50 - 50 * (baseline - rent_to_income) / (baseline - min(rent_to_income, na.rm = TRUE))
    )
  )

# Filter for Albany, GA Metro Area and prepare year
metro_data <- combined_data %>%
  filter(NAME == "Albany, GA Metro Area") %>%
  mutate(

#Prepare and join

# Fixing join keys (PERMITS has CBSA; POPULATION has GEOID)
# Making sure both sides use the same type; tidycensus GEOID is typically numeric for CBSA
PERMITS_fixed <- PERMITS %>%
  rename(GEOID = CBSA) %>%
  mutate(GEOID = as.numeric(GEOID))  # if POPULATION$GEOID is character, change to as.character()

# Join population & permits
hg <- POPULATION %>%
  mutate(GEOID = as.numeric(GEOID)) %>%            # match type to PERMITS_fixed
  inner_join(PERMITS_fixed, by = c("GEOID", "year")) %>%
  mutate(NAME = enc2utf8(NAME)) %>%
  arrange(GEOID, year)

# 5-year population growth (starts in 2014)
hg <- hg %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  mutate(
    pop_5yrs_ago     = dplyr::lag(population, 5),
    pop_growth_count = population - pop_5yrs_ago,
    pop_growth_rate  = pop_growth_count / pop_5yrs_ago   # e.g., 0.07 = +7% over 5 yrs
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Two housing-growth metrics
# (a) Instantaneous: permits per 1,000 residents this year
# (b) Rate-based: permits per person of 5-year population growth (only when growth > 0)
hg <- hg %>%
  mutate(
    inst_growth = (new_housing_units_permitted / pmax(population, 1)) * 1000,
    rate_denom  = dplyr::if_else(is.na(pop_growth_count) | pop_growth_count <= 0, NA_real_, pop_growth_count * 1.0),
    rate_growth = new_housing_units_permitted / rate_denom
  )

# Standardizing each metric on 0–100
hg <- hg %>%
  mutate(
    inst_index = rescale(inst_growth, to = c(0, 100), na.rm = TRUE),
    rate_index = rescale(rate_growth, to = c(0, 100), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Composite index (equal-weight average of the two indices)
hg <- hg %>%
  mutate(
    composite_index = rowMeans(cbind(inst_index, rate_index), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#formatting for tables
last_year <- max(hg$year, na.rm = TRUE)

pretty_tbl <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    transmute(
      `Metro Area` = NAME,
      Year         = year,
      Population   = population,
      Permits      = new_housing_units_permitted,
      `5-yr Pop Growth (%)` = pop_growth_rate * 100,
      `Instantaneous Growth (permits per 1k)`     = inst_growth,
      `Rate-based Growth (permits / 5-yr pop add)`= rate_growth,
      `Instantaneous Index (0–100)` = inst_index,
      `Rate-based Index (0–100)`     = rate_index,
      `Composite Index (0–100)`      = composite_index
    )
}

fmt_dt <- function(dtobj) {
  dtobj |>
    formatRound(c("Population","Permits"), digits = 0) |>
    formatPercentage("5-yr Pop Growth (%)", digits = 1) |>
    formatRound("Instantaneous Growth (permits per 1k)", digits = 2) |>
    formatRound("Rate-based Growth (permits / 5-yr pop add)", digits = 2) |>
    formatRound(c("Instantaneous Index (0–100)",
                  "Rate-based Index (0–100)",
                  "Composite Index (0–100)"), digits = 2)
}

# Rankings for the latest year
hg_latest <- hg %>% filter(year == last_year)
inst_rank <- hg_latest %>% arrange(desc(inst_index))

# Prepare top 10 and bottom 10 with highlight flags (use inst_index from inst_rank)
inst_top10_raw <- head(inst_rank, 10) %>%
  mutate(highlight_flag = if_else(inst_index == max(inst_index, na.rm = TRUE), "highest", ""))

inst_bottom10_raw <- tail(inst_rank, 10) %>%
  mutate(highlight_flag = if_else(inst_index == min(inst_index, na.rm = TRUE), "lowest", ""))

#pretty display tables, keep the highlight_flag column for styling
inst_top10 <- pretty_tbl(inst_top10_raw) %>%
  mutate(highlight_flag = inst_top10_raw$highlight_flag)

inst_bottom10 <- pretty_tbl(inst_bottom10_raw) %>%
  mutate(highlight_flag = inst_bottom10_raw$highlight_flag)

#compute 0-based target index for the highlight column to hide it
hide_target <- function(df, colname = "highlight_flag") {
  which(names(df) == colname) - 1  
}

# Create DT for TOP 10 (highlighting the single 'highest' row)
dt_inst_high <- datatable(
  inst_top10,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10,
    autoWidth = TRUE,
    columnDefs = list(list(visible = FALSE, targets = hide_target(inst_top10, "highlight_flag")))
  ),
  caption = tags$caption(
    style = 'caption-side: top; text-align: left; font-weight: bold;',
    paste0("Instantaneous Housing Growth — Highest 10 (", last_year, ")")
  )
) %>%
  # Use the highlight_flag values to style entire rows
  formatStyle(
    columns = names(inst_top10),                        
    target = "row",
    valueColumns = "highlight_flag",
    backgroundColor = styleEqual(c("highest"), c("#1f77b4")),
    color = styleEqual(c("highest"), c("white")),
    fontWeight = styleEqual(c("highest"), c("bold"))

  ) %>%
  inner_join(POPULATION %>% select(GEOID, year, NAME, population),
             by = c("GEOID", "year"))

# Example: compute housing growth metrics
housing_growth_data <- POPULATION %>%
  inner_join(PERMITS, by = c("GEOID" = "CBSA", "year")) %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(
    permits_per_1k = new_housing_units_permitted / population * 1000
  ) %>%
  ungroup()




Show code
yimby_analysis <- rent_burden_data %>%
  group_by(GEOID, NAME) %>%
  summarise(
    rent_burden_2009 = rent_burden_index[year == 2009],
    rent_burden_latest = rent_burden_index[year == max(year)],
    rent_burden_change = rent_burden_latest - rent_burden_2009,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  inner_join(
    housing_growth_data %>%
      group_by(GEOID, NAME) %>%
      summarise(
        total_pop_growth = last(population) - first(population),
        pop_growth_rate = (last(population) - first(population)) / first(population) * 100,
        avg_permits_per_1k = mean(permits_per_1k, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    by = c("GEOID", "NAME")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    high_early_burden = rent_burden_2009 > median(rent_burden_2009, na.rm = TRUE),
    burden_decreased = rent_burden_change < 0,
    pop_grew = total_pop_growth > 0,
    above_avg_housing = avg_permits_per_1k > median(avg_permits_per_1k, na.rm = TRUE),
    yimby_score = as.integer(high_early_burden) +
                  as.integer(burden_decreased) +
                  as.integer(pop_grew) +
                  as.integer(above_avg_housing),
    is_yimby = yimby_score == 4
  )

text:
This mini project for STA 9750 examines housing affordability which is a major challenge in cities in the United States especially New York City. The goal is to identify cities most supportive of new housing development or YIMBY by analyzing census and real estate data.
The results will be used to create a short policy brief to guide politicians in supporting a federal YIMBY incentive program and highlight districts that could benefit from these policies.
This project helps students strengthen skills in data analysis critical thinking and communication by using advanced data manipulation, creating clear visualizations, and presenting complex information in an understandable way.

title: Mini-Project #02 — Making Backyards Affordable for All
text:
Policy Brief
Objective: Encourage cities to adopt housing-friendly policies that increase supply, lower rent burden, and support population growth.
Proposed Sponsors:
Primary Sponsor: Wilmington, NC – a YIMBY success story showing decreased rent burden, population growth, and strong housing development.
Co-Sponsor: Danville, IL – a NIMBY/low-growth city highlighting where policy incentives are needed.
Rationale: Wilmington demonstrates that affordability and growth can coexist. Danville highlights the risks of restricted housing supply, where rents remain high despite population stagnation.
Targeted Support from Occupations:
Wilmington, NC: Teachers, Firefighters – benefit from lower housing costs, stronger labor support for policy.
Danville, IL: Nurses, Police Officers – benefit from potential rent reduction, financial stability, and union support for legislation.
Metrics to Identify YIMBY Cities:
Rent Burden Index: Shows affordability trends relative to income.
Housing Growth Metric: Measures permits per population to capture active development.
Composite Score: Combines rent burden improvement and housing growth to flag successful YIMBY metros.
Conclusion: Cities scoring high on YIMBY criteria are ideal for federal program pilots. Supporting local housing expansion benefits residents, strengthens local economies, and gains political and labor support.

Project Overview This project focuses on revitalizing District 42 by replacing dead trees and increasing overall tree coverage. The aim is to enhance the neighborhood environment, promote community well-being, and create a more inviting space for both residents and visitors. Through tree replacement and new plantings, the district will benefit from a healthier, greener, and more sustainable urban landscape.
District Selection Data analysis reveals that District 42 has one of the highest proportions of dead trees in the city, approximately 14% of its total tree population. Concentrating efforts here will have a significant positive impact on the area’s public spaces and overall urban greenery.
Goals and Scope
Replace 100 dead trees to improve safety and maintain a vibrant streetscape.
Plant 200 new trees to enhance biodiversity and increase green coverage.
New plantings will help cool streets during summer heatwaves, improve air quality, manage stormwater, and create shaded, enjoyable public areas.
Overall, the project contributes to environmental sustainability, neighborhood aesthetics, and property value enhancement.

Clicking on individual trees provides information about each one, including species and basic maintenance requirements.
The map makes it simple to identify areas with greater shade and tree coverage, as well as neighborhoods that may experience higher temperatures and poorer air quality due to fewer trees. NYC Parks Proposal: Reviving the Canopy in Brooklyn’s Council District 42
Strengthening Brooklyn’s Urban Forest: Council District 42
Brooklyn’s Council District 42 faces a pressing challenge: a significant portion of its street trees are in poor condition. Analysis of NYC’s street tree dataset reveals tne of the highest rates among all city council districts. While other districts, like Staten Island’s District 50 or Manhattan’s District 10, host more trees overall, their mortality rates are considerably lower. This indicates a clear need for targeted intervention in District 42.
Project Overview: “Reviving the Urban Canopy”
Purpose: Enhance the health, safety, and beauty of Brooklyn’s streets by reducing tree mortality and expanding green coverage.
Three-Year Goals:
Replace 500 dead or critically endangered trees.
Plant 800 new trees in areas with sparse greenery.
Lower the dead-tree rate to under 10% within five years.
Visual Insights District Map Highlight
A detailed map of District 42 shows all street trees as colored points: green for healthy trees and red for dead ones. This visual highlights areas with high tree mortality, helping planners prioritize locations for maintenance and planting.
Comparative Tree Analysis
A bar chart illustrates both total tree numbers and the fraction of dead trees for several districts:
Brooklyn District 42 (focus)
Staten Island District 50 (many trees, low mortality)
Manhattan District 10 (dense canopy, healthier trees)
Manhattan District 2 (Baruch College area)
This comparison demonstrates that District 42 has a disproportionally high rate of tree loss compared to other well-planted districts, emphasizing the urgency of intervention.
Recommended Actions
Tree Removal & Replacement: Focus on streets or blocks with clusters of dead trees.
Replanting Programs: Use species resilient to urban pollution and climate stress.
Tree Risk Assessments: Inspect large or vulnerable trees to prevent accidents.
Community Engagement: Organize a “Giving Tree Day” to educate and involve local residents in caring for new trees.
Strategic Importance
District 42 is not the district with the most trees, but it has one of the highest mortality rates. Clustered areas of dead trees compromise street aesthetics, shade availability, and public safety. By focusing resources here, we can rapidly enhance the urban canopy, improve environmental quality, and align the district’s tree health with healthier districts like Staten Island 50, Manhattan 10, and Manhattan 2.
